title: Security Boundary and Trust Diagram
purpose: Define four concentric trust zones from trusted internal server network to external untrusted actors and map data flows across each boundary, highlighting XSS, JWT storage, and sandbox bypass risks.
audience: Security engineers, backend developers, architects, compliance team
description: Four concentric trust zones: Zone 1 (Trusted Internal, dark green) — Express Server Process, Supabase PostgreSQL, server-side environment variables. Zone 2 (Partially Trusted, yellow-green) — Cloudflare R2 storage, Stripe API, Ethereum RPC Base network, OpenRouter/OpenAI API. Zone 3 (Untrusted Client, light red) — Browser React SPA, localStorage/sessionStorage (JWT stored here), mobile/HTTP clients. Zone 4 (External Actors, red) — end users (fans, creators), admin users (elevated privileges but same untrusted client), third-party attackers. Key risk vectors: JWTs in localStorage susceptible to XSS attacks, R2 signed URLs crossing trust boundaries, sandbox bypass where fake 0x0000 txHash from untrusted client skips on-chain verification, AI caption sending base64 images to OpenAI without user consent.

Authentication and authorization middleware is active
Environment variables are configured with secrets and API keys

Security risks at each boundary are documented

validationRules: All external API calls must use HTTPS with proper certificate validation
JWT should ideally be stored in httpOnly cookies, not localStorage
Sandbox mode must never reach production environment
User consent must be obtained before sending data to third-party AI APIs
securityConsiderations: CRITICAL: JWT in localStorage is vulnerable to XSS — any injected script can exfiltrate tokens
CRITICAL: Sandbox 0x0000 bypass allows any authenticated user to create verified transactions without real on-chain proof
HIGH: AI caption sends base64 image data to OpenAI/OpenRouter without explicit user consent
HIGH: R2 signed URLs cross trust boundaries — generated in Zone 1, consumed in Zone 3 (browser)
MEDIUM: Admin users operate from the same untrusted client as regular users — elevated privileges on untrusted device
